claim: Microbes often exist in spatially structured environments.
source: Microbes often exist in spatially structured environments and many of their interactions are mediated through diffusible metabolites.
evidence: This is a general statement about microbial ecology presented in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Many microbial interactions are mediated through diffusible metabolites.
source: Microbes often exist in spatially structured environments and many of their interactions are mediated through diffusible metabolites.
evidence: This is a general statement about microbial interactions presented in the abstract as established knowledge.

claim: Slower motility of cells promotes coexistence by allowing species to co-localize with their facilitators and avoid their inhibitors.
source: In our model, we find that slower motility of cells promotes coexistence by allowing species to co-localize with their facilitators and avoid their inhibitors.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A spatially structured environment is more influential when species mostly facilitate each other, rather than when they are mostly competing.
source: We additionally find that a spatially structured environment is more influential when species mostly facilitate each other, rather than when they are mostly competing.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: More coexistence is observed when species produce many mediators and consume some (not many or few) mediators.
source: More coexistence is observed when species produce many mediators and consume some (not many or few) mediators, and when overall consumption and production rates are balanced.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: More coexistence is observed when overall consumption and production rates are balanced.
source: More coexistence is observed when species produce many mediators and consume some (not many or few) mediators, and when overall consumption and production rates are balanced.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Coexistence appears to be disfavored when mediators are diffusing slowly because that leads to weaker interaction strengths.
source: Interestingly, coexistence appears to be disfavored when mediators are diffusing slowly because that leads to weaker interaction strengths.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: Microbes are rarely found in isolation in nature.
source: Microbes are rarely found in isolation in nature.
evidence: This is a general statement about microbial ecology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Microbes are found coexisting with one another in complex networks of interactions.
source: Instead, they are found coexisting with one another in complex networks of interactions (Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2020.

claim: Many important industrial, environmental, and health-related processes rely on microbial communities to function.
source: And because many important industrial, environmental, and health-related processes rely on microbial communities to function (e.g. anaerobic granules, microbial mats, and gut microbiota, respectively), understanding the conditions that favor microbial coexistence is critical to sustaining these systems.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with examples provided.

claim: Understanding the conditions that favor microbial coexistence is critical to sustaining industrial, environmental, and health-related systems.
source: And because many important industrial, environmental, and health-related processes rely on microbial communities to function (e.g. anaerobic granules, microbial mats, and gut microbiota, respectively), understanding the conditions that favor microbial coexistence is critical to sustaining these systems.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the importance of microbial communities to these systems.

claim: Spatial structure and organization may shape coexistence via numerous mechanisms.
source: Spatial structure and organization may shape coexistence via numerous mechanisms (Tilman, 1994; Durrett and Levin, 1994; Tilman and Kareiva, 1998; Durrett and Levin, 1998; Kerr et al., 2002; Brockhurst et al., 2006; Amarasekare, 2003), often by modulating the interactions among individuals.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Spatial structure often shapes coexistence by modulating the interactions among individuals.
source: Spatial structure and organization may shape coexistence via numerous mechanisms (Tilman, 1994; Durrett and Levin, 1994; Tilman and Kareiva, 1998; Durrett and Levin, 1998; Kerr et al., 2002; Brockhurst et al., 2006; Amarasekare, 2003), often by modulating the interactions among individuals.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In a spatially structured environment where progeny is more likely to be in the vicinity of parents, intensified intrapopulation competition can give less competitive species a chance to survive.
source: For example, in a spatially structured environment where progeny is more likely to be in the vicinity of parents, intensified intrapopulation competition can give less competitive species a chance to survive (Chesson, 2000a).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Chesson, 2000a.

claim: Spatial isolation can allow organisms with conflicting abiotic needs to flourish in appropriate environments.
source: In other conditions, spatial isolation can allow organisms with conflicting abiotic needs to flourish in appropriate environments (Kim et al., 2011; Satoh et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2011 and Satoh et al., 2007.

claim: The interplay between dispersal and competition can allow coexistence between species that are more competitive growers and species that are better at dispersing and colonizing.
source: The interplay between dispersal and competition can also allow coexistence between species that are more competitive growers and species that are better at dispersing and colonizing (Tilman, 1990).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tilman, 1990.

claim: Spatial heterogeneity has been invoked as a mechanism for microbial coexistence since the pioneering work by Gause, 1934.
source: Spatial heterogeneity has been invoked as a mechanism for microbial coexistence since the pioneering work by Gause, 1934.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gause, 1934.

claim: General concepts of coexistence are expected to apply equally to microbes.
source: And although general concepts of coexistence are expected to apply equally to microbes, microbial communities may be affected by spatial structure in unique ways because of the scale and multiplicity of microbial interactions.
evidence: This is presented as a general expectation in the field.

claim: Microbial communities may be affected by spatial structure in unique ways because of the scale and multiplicity of microbial interactions.
source: And although general concepts of coexistence are expected to apply equally to microbes, microbial communities may be affected by spatial structure in unique ways because of the scale and multiplicity of microbial interactions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the unique characteristics of microbial communities.

claim: Spatial structure can stabilize microbial interactions mediated via diffusible metabolites and support coexistence by allowing cheaters to be excluded from beneficial interactions.
source: Spatial structure can stabilize these interactions and support coexistence, for example, by allowing cheaters to be excluded from beneficial interactions (Momeni et al., 2013b; Pande et al., 2016), or by permitting facilitative chemical interactions while preventing the inhibitory effects of an interacting organism's physical presence (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Momeni et al., 2013b and Pande et al., 2016.

claim: Spatial structure can support coexistence by permitting facilitative chemical interactions while preventing the inhibitory effects of an interacting organism's physical presence.
source: Spatial structure can stabilize these interactions and support coexistence, for example, by allowing cheaters to be excluded from beneficial interactions (Momeni et al., 2013b; Pande et al., 2016), or by permitting facilitative chemical interactions while preventing the inhibitory effects of an interacting organism's physical presence (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claim: The outcomes of interactions via diffusible mediators in structured environments may depend on mediator diffusion rates.
source: And while it is clear that the outcomes of interactions via diffusible mediators in structured environments may depend on mediator diffusion rates (Kümmerli et al., 2014; Allison, 2005) and the larger network of antagonistic and cooperative interactions (Nadell et al., 2016), how such factors translate into community-level consequences is not well understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kümmerli et al., 2014 and Allison, 2005.

claim: The outcomes of interactions via diffusible mediators in structured environments may depend on the larger network of antagonistic and cooperative interactions.
source: And while it is clear that the outcomes of interactions via diffusible mediators in structured environments may depend on mediator diffusion rates (Kümmerli et al., 2014; Allison, 2005) and the larger network of antagonistic and cooperative interactions (Nadell et al., 2016), how such factors translate into community-level consequences is not well understood.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nadell et al., 2016.

claim: How mediator diffusion rates and interaction networks translate into community-level consequences is not well understood.
source: And while it is clear that the outcomes of interactions via diffusible mediators in structured environments may depend on mediator diffusion rates (Kümmerli et al., 2014; Allison, 2005) and the larger network of antagonistic and cooperative interactions (Nadell et al., 2016), how such factors translate into community-level consequences is not well understood.
evidence: This is presented as a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Prior reports that address coexistence of metabolically interacting microbes in a spatially structured environment are scarce.
source: Prior reports that address coexistence of metabolically interacting microbes in a spatially structured environment are scarce.
evidence: This is presented as an assessment of the existing literature.

claim: Murrell and Law, 2003 showed in a modified Lotka–Volterra model that when interspecific competition operates over shorter distances than intraspecific competition a spatially structured environment can lead to species coexistence by allowing for aggregation.
source: In an implicit model, Murrell and Law, 2003 have shown in a modified Lotka–Volterra model that when interspecific competition operates over shorter distances than intraspecific competition a spatially structured environment can lead to species coexistence by allowing for aggregation.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Murrell and Law, 2003.

claim: Weiner et al., 2019 found that metabolic tradeoffs allow for the coexistence of more species than the number of nutrients in territorial populations interacting through diffusible mediators.
source: And in recent work with explicit modeling of space, Weiner et al., 2019 examined coexistence in territorial populations interacting through diffusible mediators and found that metabolic tradeoffs allow for the coexistence of more species than the number of nutrients.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Weiner et al., 2019.

claim: The model in this study is distinct from previous work in that it allows overlap and dispersal of populations through the shared space.
source: Our model is distinct from previous work in that we allow overlap and dispersal of populations through the shared space.
evidence: This is a description of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mucosal layer of the digestive or respiratory tract is an example where microbes can disperse inside a matrix that defines the spatial structure.
source: Our motivation is to capture situations in which microbes can disperse inside a matrix that defines the spatial structure. An example of this is the mucosal layer of the digestive or respiratory tract, in which stratification is possible, yet the distribution of different species populations can overlap.
evidence: This is presented as an example of a biological system that the model aims to capture.

claim: In the mucosal layer of the digestive or respiratory tract, stratification is possible, yet the distribution of different species populations can overlap.
source: An example of this is the mucosal layer of the digestive or respiratory tract, in which stratification is possible, yet the distribution of different species populations can overlap.
evidence: This is presented as a characteristic of the mucosal layer.

claim: Yogurt or cheese are examples where spatial structure exists, but populations are not territorial.
source: Another example is in yogurt or cheese, where spatial structure exists, but populations are not territorial.
evidence: This is presented as an example of a biological system that the model aims to capture.

claim: The study limits its investigation to one-dimensional (1D) spatial structure as a starting point.
source: We modify a previously developed mediator-explicit model (Niehaus et al., 2019) to account for spatial structure and the dispersion of species in the same space. Here, we limit our study to one-dimensional (1D) spatial structure as a starting point.
evidence: This is a description of the model scope presented in the manuscript.

claim: The purpose of this work is not to recapture a specific community.
source: We should emphasize that even though we choose our parameters within the range of typical values observed among microbial communities, the purpose of this work is not to recapture a specific community.
evidence: This is a statement about the goals of the study.

claim: The study aims to gain a better understanding of how rates of metabolite diffusion and species dispersal can affect species coexistence.
source: Instead, by examining a range of values for parameters such as metabolite diffusion and species dispersal, we hope to gain a better understanding of how rates of these processes can affect species coexistence.
evidence: This is a statement about the goals of the study.

claim: In the mediator-explicit model, species interact through metabolites that they produce and/or consume.
source: In our mediator-explicit model, species interact through metabolites that they produce and/or consume (Figure 1A, B; Niehaus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the model presented in the manuscript, supported by Figure 1A, B and a citation to Niehaus et al., 2019.

claim: Each species can produce a subset of metabolites and consume a subset of metabolites.
source: Each species can produce a subset of metabolites and consume a subset of metabolites.
evidence: This is a description of the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each of the metabolites in the shared environment can influence any of the species by increasing or decreasing their growth rate compared to how each species grows in the absence of interactions.
source: Each of the metabolites in the shared environment can in turn influence any of the species by increasing or decreasing their growth rate (i.e. facilitation or inhibition, respectively) compared to how each species grows in the absence of interactions (Niehaus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the model presented in the manuscript, supported by a citation to Niehaus et al., 2019.

claim: Different interaction mediators additively influence the overall growth rate of each species.
source: We also assume that different interaction mediators additively influence the overall growth rate of each species (see Model description in Methods).
evidence: This is a description of an assumption in the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Similar to a well-mixed environment, more facilitative interactions lead to higher richness in communities that emerge from enrichment in spatial environments.
source: Our results show that, similar to a well-mixed environment, more facilitative interactions lead to higher richness in communities that emerge from enrichment (Figure 1C, along the x-axis).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Spatial communities show more coexistence than well-mixed communities when facilitation among species is prevalent.
source: Additionally, we observe that spatial communities show more coexistence than well-mixed communities when facilitation among species is prevalent (Figure 1C, spatial versus well-mixed).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Species locally grow better when adjacent to a facilitative partner and grow worse when in the vicinity of an inhibitory partner.
source: Our explanation is that species locally grow better when adjacent to a facilitative partner and grow worse when in the vicinity of an inhibitory partner.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: Spatial self-organization in effect amplifies facilitative interactions and dampens inhibitory interactions, leading to more coexistence.
source: The resulting spatial self-organization in effect amplifies facilitative interactions and dampens inhibitory interactions, leading to more coexistence.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: The position of specific species with respect to other species that facilitate or inhibit it can impact the population dynamics.
source: This is supported by our data which shows that the position of specific species with respect to other species that facilitate or inhibit it can impact the population dynamics (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: There is more similarity between well-mixed and spatial communities in the absence of strong facilitative interactions.
source: As a result, there is more similarity between well-mixed and spatial communities in the absence of strong facilitative interactions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: Coexistence is favored when the number of metabolites produced is larger.
source: We found that coexistence is favored when the number of metabolites produced is larger (Figure 2, along the y-axis).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The effect of larger number of metabolites produced on coexistence was stronger when the metabolite influences were mostly facilitative.
source: This effect was stronger when the metabolite influences were mostly facilitative (fac:inh = 90:10, versus 50:50 or 10:90).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Coexistence achieved its maximum values at intermediate ranges of mediator influence.
source: In contrast, coexistence achieved its maximum values at intermediate ranges of mediator influence (Figure 2, x-axis), that is lower coexistence was observed when each mediator influenced too many or too few species on average.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Lower coexistence was observed when each mediator influenced too many or too few species on average.
source: In contrast, coexistence achieved its maximum values at intermediate ranges of mediator influence (Figure 2, x-axis), that is lower coexistence was observed when each mediator influenced too many or too few species on average.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: The trends in how production and mediator influence affect coexistence were largely the same between spatial and well-mixed communities.
source: We note that these trends were largely the same between spatial and well-mixed communities.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the model results for spatial and well-mixed communities.

claim: A larger range of production offers more opportunities for interaction, which through the enrichment process lead to the selection of facilitative subsets that coexist.
source: Our explanation is that a larger range of production offers more opportunities for interaction, which through the enrichment process lead to the selection of facilitative subsets that coexist (Niehaus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics and supported by a citation to Niehaus et al., 2019.

claim: A low mediator influence range reduces opportunities for interactions and results in lower coexistence.
source: A low mediator influence range works in the opposite direction, reduces opportunities for interactions and results in lower coexistence.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: Very high mediator influence range potentially leads to more self-facilitation, which can lead to take-over by a single species and a lower coexistence as a result.
source: Very high mediator influence range potentially leads to more self-facilitation (i.e. producing a metabolite that is beneficial to the producer species), which our data suggest can lead to take-over by a single species and a lower coexistence as a result (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The highest levels of coexistence occurred when there was a balance between consumption and production rates among species, with slightly higher production than consumption.
source: We observed that the highest levels of coexistence occurred when there was a balance between consumption and production rates among species, with slightly higher production than consumption (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: When production is too high, mediators will build up in the environment, putting the community in a regime in which consumption is not enough to create a feedback, leading to lower coexistence.
source: Our justification for the observed pattern is that in one extreme where production is too high (lower right corner of each plot), mediators will build up in the environment. This will put the community in a regime in which consumption is not enough to create a feedback, that is 'reusable mediators' as discussed in Niehaus et al., 2019, which leads to lower coexistence.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics and supported by a citation to Niehaus et al., 2019.

claim: When consumption is too high, metabolites that mediate the interactions will be depleted from the environment, leading to an effectively weaker interaction and thus lower coexistence.
source: In the other extreme, when consumption is too high (upper left corner of each plot), metabolites that mediate the interactions will be depleted from the environment, leading to an effectively weaker interaction and thus lower coexistence.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: When production is slightly higher than consumption, metabolite quantities are sufficient to create strong interactions and facilitation feedbacks, leading to higher coexistence.
source: However, when production is slightly higher than consumption, metabolite quantities are sufficient to create strong interactions and facilitation feedbacks, leading to higher coexistence.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: Coexistence is slightly higher in the spatial communities compared to well-mixed ones when examining production and consumption rates.
source: While coexistence is slightly higher in the spatial communities compared to well-mixed ones, the production–consumption trends apply equally to spatial and well-mixed communities, as expected.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the model results for spatial and well-mixed communities.

claim: The production–consumption trends apply equally to spatial and well-mixed communities.
source: While coexistence is slightly higher in the spatial communities compared to well-mixed ones, the production–consumption trends apply equally to spatial and well-mixed communities, as expected.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the model results for spatial and well-mixed communities.

claim: When the diffusion coefficient for species approaches zero and cells remain in their original spatial location, higher levels of coexistence are observed.
source: When the diffusion coefficient for species approaches zero and cells remain in their original spatial location, we observe higher levels of coexistence (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The impact of lower dispersal is stronger in communities in which most interactions are facilitative rather than inhibitory.
source: We also observed that the impact of lower dispersal is stronger in communities in which most interactions are facilitative rather than inhibitory.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Lower dispersal rates mean that species grow best in spatial locations that are more supportive for their growth, which is in the vicinity of their beneficial partners and away from competitors or inhibitors.
source: Our explanation is that lower dispersal rates mean that species grow best in spatial locations that are more supportive for their growth, which is in the vicinity of their beneficial partners and away from competitors or inhibitors.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: As the dispersal coefficient increases, the self-organization gets washed away by dispersal of cells to less than ideal locations for their growth and its benefit for coexistence diminishes.
source: As the dispersal coefficient increases, the self-organization gets washed away by dispersal of cells to less than ideal locations for their growth and its benefit for coexistence diminishes.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: At intermediate levels of dispersal, the trend reversed and well-mixed communities showed more coexistence compared to spatial communities.
source: At intermediate levels of dispersal, the trend reversed and well-mixed communities showed more coexistence compared to spatial communities.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: At the limit of extremely rapid diffusion, when the species distribution is kept uniform across the spatial extent, coexistence outcomes matched the well-mixed case.
source: This is interesting because at the limit of extremely rapid diffusion (shown with a '∞' sign in Figure 4) when we kept the species distribution uniform across the spatial extent, coexistence outcomes matched the well-mixed case, as expected.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: At intermediate levels of dispersal, the spatial distribution of populations is still changing considerably even after 100 generations.
source: The first contribution came from longer-term changes in dynamics at intermediate levels of dispersal. Even after 100 generations, which is the typical extent of our studies, at intermediate levels of dispersal (e.g. DCell = 5 × 10−6 cm2/hr), the spatial distribution of populations is still changing considerably.
evidence: This is an observation from the model simulations.

claim: The strict criteria for stable coexistence removes some of the populations that are still temporally not stable enough at intermediate dispersal levels, leading to a lower overall assessment of coexistence in these cases.
source: As a result, our strict criteria for stable coexistence removes some of the populations that are still temporally not stable enough, leading to a lower overall assessment of coexistence in these cases.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics and the coexistence criteria used.

claim: Self-facilitation interactions contribute to the decrease in coexistence at intermediate dispersal levels.
source: As a second factor, we hypothesized that self-facilitation interactions contribute to the decrease in coexistence at intermediate dispersal levels.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the model simulations, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Self-facilitation interactions are amplified in communities in which the spatial context is preserved, because the distribution of producers matches the distribution of self, but not other recipients.
source: Our rationale was that self-facilitation interactions are amplified in communities in which the spatial context is preserved, because the distribution of producers matches the distribution of self, but not other recipients in such a case.
evidence: This is an explanation for the hypothesized mechanism.

claim: Amplification of self-facilitation can lead to community overtake by a self-facilitating species.
source: This can lead to community overtake by a self-facilitating species.
evidence: This is an explanation for the hypothesized mechanism.

claim: Weaker self-facilitation links led to higher coexistence in communities with intermediate dispersal coefficients but not in well-mixed communities or communities with low dispersal coefficients.
source: To test this, we tested weaker self-facilitation links in our simulations and observed that this change led to higher coexistence in communities with intermediate dispersal coefficients but not in well-mixed communities or communities with low dispersal coefficients (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Higher mean richness is typically observed for spatial communities compared with the well-mixed communities over a range of mediator diffusion coefficients.
source: We still typically observe a higher mean richness for spatial communities compared with the well-mixed communities (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: As the diffusion of mediators becomes slower, coexistence in spatial communities decreases.
source: However, unlike the conventional wisdom, as the diffusion of mediators becomes slower, coexistence in spatial communities decreases.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: At low diffusion coefficients, coexistence drops even below that of corresponding well-mixed communities.
source: At low diffusion coefficients, coexistence drops even below that of corresponding well-mixed communities.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in the manuscript, supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The trend of decreased coexistence at lower mediator diffusion is associated with weaker effective interactions among species at lower diffusion coefficients.
source: We associate this trend to weaker effective interactions among species at lower diffusion coefficients.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: Mediators that are involved in facilitation play a major part in allowing coexistence of species.
source: Mediators that are involved in facilitation play a major part in allowing coexistence of species (Niehaus et al., 2019); if these mediators get consumed by nearby species and do not travel long enough to reach other members of the community, the interaction-driven mechanism of coexistence is disrupted.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Niehaus et al., 2019.

claim: If facilitative mediators get consumed by nearby species and do not travel long enough to reach other members of the community, the interaction-driven mechanism of coexistence is disrupted.
source: Mediators that are involved in facilitation play a major part in allowing coexistence of species (Niehaus et al., 2019); if these mediators get consumed by nearby species and do not travel long enough to reach other members of the community, the interaction-driven mechanism of coexistence is disrupted.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern, based on the model dynamics.

claim: A spatially structured environment will not universally lead to more coexistence compared to a well-mixed environment.
source: Our results dispel the common presumption that a spatially structured environment will universally lead to more coexistence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: Compared to a well-mixed environment, a spatial environment can favor or disfavor coexistence depending on the balance between species dispersal and the diffusion of interaction mediators.
source: We find that, compared to a well-mixed environment, a spatial environment can favor or disfavor coexistence depending on the balance between species dispersal and the diffusion of interaction mediators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: A lower species dispersal rate favors coexistence, but this effect can be diminished or even reversed if accompanied by low mediator diffusion rates.
source: Interestingly, a lower species dispersal rate favors coexistence, but this effect can be diminished or even reversed if accompanied by low mediator diffusion rates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: Coexistence is favored when species have a broad range of consumption and an intermediate range of production of interaction mediators.
source: Coexistence is favored when species have a broad range of consumption and an intermediate range of production of interaction mediators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: More coexistence is predicted when there is a balance between overall production and consumption rates for mediators.
source: Additionally, we predict more coexistence when there is a balance between overall production and consumption rates for mediators.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The spatial structure of microbial communities has been extensively studied for example in simulating the development of biofilms.
source: The spatial structure of microbial communities has been extensively studied for example in simulating the development of biofilms (Wang and Zhang, 2010; Kreft et al., 2001; Xavier and Foster, 2007; von der Schulenburg et al., 2009), for specific interactions among species (Momeni et al., 2013b; Momeni et al., 2013a; Kang et al., 2014), or for modeling game-theory dynamics (Nakamaru et al., 1997; Brauchli et al., 1999; Saxer et al., 2009; Hauert and Doebeli, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: There is often a tradeoff between the incorporation of detailed mechanisms and generality of conclusions in modeling.
source: However, as there is often a tradeoff between the incorporation of detailed mechanisms and generality of conclusions (Levins, 1966; Momeni et al., 2011), we chose in this work to explore a simple, general model of chemically mediated microbial interactions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Levins, 1966 and Momeni et al., 2011.

claim: The study chose to explore a simple, general model of chemically mediated microbial interactions.
source: However, as there is often a tradeoff between the incorporation of detailed mechanisms and generality of conclusions (Levins, 1966; Momeni et al., 2011), we chose in this work to explore a simple, general model of chemically mediated microbial interactions.
evidence: This is a statement about the modeling approach taken in the study.

claim: The model assumes that mediators affect species by additively influencing their growth rates.
source: We assumed, for example, that mediators affected species by additively influencing their growth rates.
evidence: This is a description of an assumption in the model.

claim: It is possible that mediator effects could be multiplicative, nonlinear, or otherwise context dependent.
source: Although it is possible (and even probable) that mediator effects could be multiplicative, nonlinear, or otherwise context dependent and that they may impact other model parameters, we chose here to present what we felt to be the simplest case.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of alternative modeling approaches.

claim: Exploration of alternative implementations of mediator effects would make a fascinating follow-up to this work.
source: Exploration of alternative implementations of mediator effects would make a fascinating follow-up to this work.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The model assumes no carrying capacity limit for the growth of populations.
source: For example, we have assumed no carrying capacity limit for the growth of our populations.
evidence: This is a description of an assumption in the model.

claim: Imposing a total population limit at each spatial location did alter the conclusions about coexistence.
source: We explored the effect of imposing a total population limit, enforced at each spatial location, and found that it did alter our conclusions (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from additional model simulations, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The relationship between carrying capacity and coexistence has been explored extensively elsewhere.
source: However, because the relationship between carrying capacity and coexistence has been explored extensively elsewhere, we chose parameters to minimize this impact, allowing us to focus on other interspecies interactions (beyond competition) and relative rates of diffusion and dispersal.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The results were largely unaffected if the community's spatial extent was changed by an order of magnitude.
source: We also tested the impact of the spatial extent of the community (Z), and observed that our results were largely unaffected if the community's spatial extent was changed by an order of magnitude (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from additional model simulations, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The effect of larger changes in the spatial extent can be examined by scaling the diffusion and dispersal coefficients accordingly.
source: The effect of larger changes in the spatial extent can be examined by scaling the diffusion and dispersal coefficients accordingly.
evidence: This is a suggestion for how to extend the analysis.

claim: There are alternative representations of interactions among species, including a simplified Lotka–Volterra model and its variations, a consumer-resource model, or a reduced metabolic model.

Interestingly, in many cases coexistence was affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that the adjacency to partners is an important determinant of spatial coexistence (as also suggested by Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).

claim: Larger changes in richness when the order of species is rearranged occur when facilitation interactions are more prevalent in the community.
source: When we examined the effect of the fac:inh ratio on these outcomes, we observed that larger changes in richness when facilitation interactions were more prevalent in the community (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), which aligns with many of our other results showing that facilitation amplifies the positive effect of spatial structure on coexistence.
evidence: This is a finding from additional model simulations, supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The impact of spatial structure on coexistence largely arises from spatial self-organization, which can improve coexistence by favoring facilitation over inhibition.
source: Overall, we believe this work revisits how spatial structure—and spatial self-organization—affects community assembly and coexistence. In our model, which emphasizes the contributions of interspecies interactions, we find that the impact of spatial structure on coexistence largely arises from two processes: (1) spatial self-organization, which can improve coexistence by favoring facilitation over inhibition, and (2) localization of interactions, which can promote coexistence in association with self-organization or hamper coexistence by slowing down and weakening species interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The study simulates community enrichment through rounds of growth and dilution for 100 generations.
source: We simulate community enrichment through rounds of growth and dilution (Niehaus et al., 2019; Goldford et al., 2018) for 100 generations, and assess the richness of each resulting community (i.e., the number of species stably persisting in the community).
evidence: This is a description of the simulation procedure, supported by citations to Niehaus et al., 2019 and Goldford et al., 2018.

claim: 100 generations of growth is often enough to reliably decide which species stably persist in the community.

evidence: This is a description of an assumption in the simulation procedure.

source: We recognize that this assumption is not universally true; however, we adopt it as an approximation, in the absence of additional information about a particular community.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the model assumption.

claim: Such a dilution preserves some of the spatial structure of the community in the next round of growth.
source: Such a dilution preserves some of the spatial structure of the community in the next round of growth and could represent a biofilm getting partially washed away by rain or in a microfluidic device, gut microbiota after a defecation event, or a broken-off portion of a granule initiating a new granule.
evidence: This is a description of the consequences of the dilution assumption and examples of biological systems it could represent.

evidence: This is a description of the comparison approach, supported by a citation to Niehaus et al., 2019.

claim: Different progressions are observed at high versus low dispersal rates, leading to different coexistence outcomes.

claim: Different population dynamics and ultimately different coexistence outcomes are observed in spatial versus well-mixed communities with the same interaction network.
source: We kept the same interaction network (A) in both spatial and well-mixed conditions and simulated the species dynamics. In the interaction network, hollow arrows indicate the flow of mediators (either production or consumption). The thickness of the lower end of each arrow shows the production rate and the thickness of the upper end of the arrow shows the strength of the mediator influence on the corresponding species. The basal growth rate of each species is shown as different shades of gray, with darker shades indicating larger basal growth rates. For spatial communities, the population density represents the sum of all densities across different spatial extents. We ran the simulation in both cases through 10 rounds of growth and dilution. Different population dynamics and ultimately different coexistence outcomes are observed in these cases after simulating 100 generations.
evidence: This is a finding from the model simulations presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.
